item.title: King Tides Threaten LA County Coast This Week: When, Where Flooding Could Be Worst
item.summary: In LA County, 5% of all land is in FEMA's high-risk flood zones. This map shows FEMA-designated flood hazard zones across Los Angeles County ...
item.page_text:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Potentially record-breaking king tides coupled with large waves are expected to cause significant coastal flooding across parts of Los Angeles County this week, with the worst conditions expected Wednesday and Thanksgiving morning.
Forecasters are warning that seawater could inundate roads, damage beachfront homes and other structures, spill over seawalls and cause significant beach erosion.
Water levels along the Los Angeles County coast are projected to peak at 8.3 feet Wednesday and 8.2 feet Thanksgiving Day, according to the National Weather Service. The greatest threat of flooding will be between 7 and 11 a.m., when tides are highest.
While moderate coastal flooding is expected Tuesday and Friday, forecasters are warning of major coastal flooding Wednesday and Thursday, when waves of 6 to 11 feet will coincide with exceptionally high tides.
Significant flooding of low-lying coastal areas is likely on those two days, with potential damage to coastal roads and structures. Beach parking lots and roads could also experience shallow flooding Tuesday and Friday.
This week's king tides could topple a record set nearly 44 years ago in Santa Monica. Water levels reached 8.5 feet on Nov. 30, 1982, during a powerful El Niño, according to federal tide gauge data. Forecasters have warned that water levels could exceed that mark along portions of the coast this week.
The areas of greatest concern in LA County are the west-facing beaches stretching from Santa Monica to the Palos Verdes Peninsula, as well as portions of Malibu, according to the NWS.
Low-lying areas of the South Bay that experienced flooding in late October are particularly vulnerable.
Flooding is also a concern within harbors and bays, where high water levels could damage docks and send seawater spilling into surrounding neighborhoods, including Naples in Long Beach.
Residents can check federal flood maps to see how their properties may be impacted. In LA County, 5% of all land is in FEMA's high-risk flood zones.
This week's king tides threaten a coastline already battered by successive rounds of destructive surf and unusually high tides since late summer.
In September, powerful swells generated by Hurricane Marie stripped away sand, damaged seawalls and forced evacuations in Malibu and Long Beach. In Malibu, coastal erosion opened a massive sinkhole near actor Nicolas Cage's beachfront home , cutting off road access to a neighborhood and forcing the evacuation of 31 properties.
Weeks later, waves generated by Tropical Storm Rachel tore apart portions of the Long Beach Peninsula's historic boardwalk and severely damaged beachfront homes. Eight buildings were deemed unsafe to enter.
Just last week, the Long Beach City Council approved a $7 million increase in an emergency coastal repair contract as the city braces for the possibility of further damage this winter.
By late October, record-setting water levels were causing problems elsewhere along the LA County coast, including in Redondo Beach, where seawater spilled onto the International Boardwalk and inundated waterfront businesses.
The loss of protective sand along stretches of the Southern California coast has raised concerns that subsequent bouts of high surf and elevated tides could inflict even more damage.
As of early Tuesday, the following weather alerts were in effect for the LA County coast:
Forecasters indicated Monday that the coastal flood watch would likely be upgraded to a warning.
A large swell out of the west will arrive Tuesday and peak Wednesday and Thursday, coinciding with the unusually high tides and worsening the threat of flooding.
Beachgoers are being urged to stay out of the ocean and off rock jetties. Powerful rip currents, waves that can sweep people off beaches and rocks and breaking waves near harbor entrances will make conditions particularly dangerous.
Residents in flood-prone coastal areas are urged to take steps to protect their property ahead of Wednesday morning. Motorists traveling along the coast should allow for extra travel time due to potential road closures and avoid driving through floodwaters.
In Long Beach, city crews have reinforced protective sand berms where possible, cleared storm drains and checked pump stations and seawall plugs. Boat owners are being urged to ensure their vessels are securely tied to docks and to avoid creating wakes in the Naples canals.
Malibu officials are urging beachfront property owners to inspect their seawalls and check for signs of erosion or structural damage when it's safe to do so.
"King tide" is an informal term for a phenomenon in which the alignment of the Earth, moon and sun produces some of the highest tides of the year.
This week's king tides are coming at a time when sea levels along the California coast are already unusually high due to a strong El Niño and an ongoing marine heat wave.
El Niño-driven ocean disturbances known as Kelvin waves have been carrying pulses of warm water toward the West Coast, temporarily raising sea levels by 6 to 12 inches or more. The marine heat wave is compounding the problem, as seawater expands when it warms, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Those conditions, combined with exceptionally high tides, pushed water levels to all-time highs in Los Angeles, Santa Barbara, San Diego and La Jolla in late October. Santa Monica recorded its second-highest water level ever.
The threat won't end with Thanksgiving. NOAA expects additional Kelvin waves to reach the California coast in the coming months and has identified Dec. 22-26 as another period of particularly high tides and an elevated risk of coastal flooding.

item.title: Georgia’s Pecan Belt
item.summary: Since an early-1900s planting boom, orchards along the Flint River in southwest Georgia have become a center of U.S. pecan production.
item.page_text:
Since an early-1900s planting boom, orchards along the Flint River in southwest Georgia have become a center of U.S. pecan production.
From the star of its namesake pie to a supporting player in countless side dishes, the pecan has earned a place on Thanksgiving tables across the United States. But before it becomes candied, chopped, or baked, it hangs from the branches of Carya illinoinensis —a species of hickory in the walnut family native to North America. Many U.S.-grown pecans come from orchards in Georgia, the state that has historically led the nation in production.
One hotspot of pecan cultivation is in the southwest part of the state, around Albany, in Dougherty County. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 captured this image of the area and neighboring counties on October 23, 2026. That date falls within the pecan harvest season, which typically runs from October into December . In addition to pecans, other crops such as peanuts, cotton, and corn are also grown in the area.
Landsat observations like these contribute to the Cropland Data Layer , an annual map of crop types across the contiguous United States produced by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Agricultural Statistics Service . The 2025 map shows pecan groves clustered along the Flint River within the Coastal Plain . Pecan trees need abundant water, and they generally do well in the area’s well-drained sandy soils that sit above the Floridan aquifer system that growers can tap for irrigation.
In the late 1800s, Georgia had less than 100 acres (40 hectares) of pecan orchards. Then, in the early 1900s, southwest Georgia’s Dougherty and Mitchell counties underwent a pecan boom when thousands of acres were planted and sold to investors . By the end of the 1950s, Georgia led the nation in pecan production, producing over 17 million pounds, according to 1959 agricultural census numbers .
In recent decades, pecan production has grown in other states, such as New Mexico and Texas. Georgia faced challenges after Hurricane Michael damaged orchards in October 2018, and Hurricane Helene dealt another blow when it swept inland in September 2024. Even so, USDA numbers show that the state’s production has topped 100 million pounds in each of the past three years (2023-2025).
In 2026, a wet summer in parts of the state helped scab take hold. The fungal disease causes brown spots on  pecan twigs, leaves, and nut shucks. Meanwhile, some growers still recovering from Hurricane Helene reported the return of a solid crop.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Kathryn Hansen.
